name: Spotlight Effect
description: People overestimate how much other people notice their appearance, mistakes, and behavior. Our own experience is so vivid to us that we assume it is much more visible to everyone else than it really is.
design_relevance_note: Useful when designing profile creation, posting, camera/microphone, or error-recovery moments: users may hesitate because they assume their awkwardness, unfinished state, or mistake will be more publicly noticed than it actually is.
prevalence_note: Widely recognized in social-product, privacy, creator, and youth-safety discussions, though less of a standard checklist heuristic than anchoring, defaults, or Hick's Law.

findings.description: Across five studies, people overestimated how much others noticed their appearance and behavior, including potentially embarrassing T-shirt choices and the prominence of their comments in a group discussion. The paper argues this comes from anchoring on one's own vivid experience and adjusting insufficiently toward other people's perspective.
findings.source_title: The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: The 'minority spotlight effect': feeling like the center of attention when a topic touches your own group
applications.description: Across three studies, members of underrepresented groups reported feeling like the center of others' attention -- and felt correspondingly negative emotions -- specifically when a topic related to their own group came up. Black participants imagined feeling most 'in the spotlight' as the only Black student in a class where a professor made a provocative group-related comment (Study 1); Black and Latino/Latina participants (Study 2) and female participants (Study 3) reported that two confederates seemed to look at them more when a recording pertained to their own group than a neutral topic, even though the confederates' actual gaze did not differ between conditions.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, disclosed experimental finding about self-consciousness tied to group identity, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no manipulator here, only a controlled study measuring a genuine perceptual bias with real social consequences for how comfortable people from marginalized groups feel in conversations about topics related to their identity.
